name: Far Western Muria
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mathew, Thomas & Rincy Mathew. 2013. Far Western Muria (Gaita Koitor Boli) Phonology Summary. SIL Language and Culture Documentation and Description 21. Dallas, Texas: SIL International. 77 pp. ISSN 1939-0785.
catalog_locator: Section 9 'Stress', p. 67; section 2.4 'Non-constrastive Stress' [sic], pp. 6-7; section 2.3, pp. 5-6; section 2.1.4, pp. 4-5; identity sections 1.1-1.3, pp. 1-2.
catalog_quote: Stress is not contrastive in Far Western Muria. Stress is phonetically realized by loudness, a rise in pitch and a slight lengthening of the vowel of the stressed syllable. Words can carry primary stress on the first syllable. And while this is particularly true for words whose first syllable nucleus is filled by a long vowel, in some sentence frames word-final syllables can carry the primary stress. In particular, with words whose first syllable nuclei are filled by short vowels and whose second syllable onset is phonetically a tap or a flap, primary stress is not only (a) carried by the word-final syllable, but also (b) the word-initial syllable loses its syllabicity and (c) the second syllable vowel is lengthened. The result in such cases is that two-syllable words are virtually reduced to a single syllable ... (At the current stage, the pronunciation of such words is variable, sometimes being pronounced as two syllables with no lengthening of the second syllable vowel, and sometimes being pronounced as a single syllable with occasional lengthening of the vowel. ...) [p. 67] ... In general, words carry primary stress on the first syllable. And while this is true, in some sentence frames and for some phonological word types primary stress is carried by the final syllable. [p. 6]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word (section 2.4: 'In general, words carry primary stress on the first syllable'). The authors' allophonic statements (medial geminate/half-long consonants after a stressed short vowel) are built on this initial-stress rule. Exception: disyllables with a short initial vowel and a tap/flap (/r/, /ṛ/) onset of the second syllable, in some sentence frames, shift primary stress to the final syllable, with the initial vowel becoming non-syllabic and the second vowel lengthening, e.g. /uṛm/ [u̯'ɽumˑ] 'louse', /taras/ [t̪ə̯'ɾas] 'snake' (p. 67); section 2.1.4 (p. 5) gives further examples of such compensatory shifts (/kuruj/ [ku'ɾuːdʒ] 'heel', /haṛap/ [ha'ɽaːp] 'cow dung').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only 'primary stress' is discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in some sentence frames for words whose first syllable has a short vowel and whose second syllable begins with a tap or flap; these words are then 'virtually reduced to a single syllable' (pp. 67-68). Pronunciation of such words is described as variable at present.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word, citation items from a wordlist, most examples from an elicited numbered list); the authors note the final-stress variant appears 'in some sentence frames', so phrase-level context conditions the exception. Compounds are not discussed for stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the variety its speakers call Gaita Koitori Boli, spoken in northern Gadchiroli and southern Gondia districts, Maharashtra (main consultant Ashok Hariram Neitham; data 2008-2010); Glottolog maps it to farw1235 / ISO fmu exactly ('Gaita Koitor Boli in Kurkheda Tehsil in Gadchiroli district = Far Western Muria [fmu]'). No dialect mismatch. Note: this is not Eastern Muria (east2340/emu) or Western Muria (west2408/mut), and the Gondi-wide 'word-initial, non-phonemic' line in van der Hulst & Goedemans 2010 (via Steever 1998) is about other Gondi varieties.

tone.translation: Gondi speakers do not speak in a single pitch; rise and fall of the voice appears in their pronunciation. This is what is called intonation (surayojan). This intonation arises in accordance with the speaker's expectations and feelings toward the listener. In the Gondi dialect intonation falls into types, as follows: 1) level (bhaka), 2) falling (mika) and 3) rising (phaka).
